title: PostgreSQL
description: Is the shared PostgreSQL (CT 130) up, healthy and not filling its disk, and is its off-site copy on Backblaze B2 current? Open it after a Postgres* alert, when an app reports database errors, and weekly to see growth and the off-site repo size.

panels.title: PostgreSQL up
panels.description: The exporter can run a query on the server (pg_up; rule PostgresDown: 0 for 2 minutes, severity from the host's tier, critical today). DOWN means every app with a database is failing. Also DOWN when the exporter itself is gone (rule TargetDown). Next: the Server log row, then 'systemctl status postgresql@18-main' in CT 130 (runbook PostgresDown).

panels.title: Connections in use
panels.description: Backends of every state over max_connections (100). Red from 80 % is rule PostgresConnectionsHigh (10 minutes): new connections are refused soon, almost always an app leaking connections or a pool set too large. The Connections panel names who holds them.

panels.title: Root disk used
panels.description: CT 130's root disk, from the Proxmox API (data, WAL, the last 3 dumps all live there). Red from 80 % is rule PostgresDiskFilling (30 minutes); at 100 % every write fails. The CT's node_exporter has no filesystem collector, so this is the only disk series. The Disk row shows the runway.

panels.title: Largest app database
panels.description: Size of the biggest application database (the postgres and template databases are left out, as the rule does). Red from 5e9 bytes is rule PostgresDatabaseLarge (1 hour): a planning signal, not an outage, half the size at which a high-volume app's tables are worth partitioning.

panels.title: Fastest growth, 24 h
panels.description: The most any application database grew in the last 24 hours (size now minus size a day ago). Red from 1e9 bytes is rule PostgresDatabaseGrowingFast (30 minutes): at that rate CT 130's free disk lasts weeks, and it fires long before PostgresDiskFilling. The rule uses delta(); this subtracts the value at offset 1d, the same quantity without the double series the new port label caused.

targets.expr: max(max by (datname) (pg_database_size_bytes{job="service", instance="postgres", datname!~"postgres|template.*"}) - max by (datname) (pg_database_size_bytes{job="service", instance="postgres", datname!~"postgres|template.*"} offset 1d))

panels.title: Off-site WAL archive age
panels.description: Time since the last WAL segment reached the B2 bucket (ADR 0034). Normal: at most 15 minutes (archive_timeout). Red from 1 hour is rule PostgresOffsiteArchiveStale (5 minutes): commits since then exist only at home. The series is a textfile written in CT 130; if it vanishes the alert is silent, so this tile shows n/a, not green.

panels.title: Newest off-site full backup
panels.description: Age of the newest full backup in the bucket (one is taken every third day at 04:00 WIB). Red from 4 days is rule PostgresOffsiteFullBackupOld (30 minutes): the restore window shrinks; WAL alone still restores, from the older full.

panels.title: Off-site repo size
panels.description: Size of the pgBackRest repo in B2 against the 10 GB free tier (steady state about 4-5 GB). Red from 8e9 bytes is rule PostgresOffsiteRepoLarge (15 minutes); at 9 GB the daily job expires down to one full backup (the guard), at 10 GB B2's $0 cap refuses writes and the archive stops.

panels.title: Is it saturated? Connections, locks, long transactions
Connections by state, against max_connections
panels.description: Backends by state (a stack: the states sum to the connections in use) against max_connections and the 80 % line that rule PostgresConnectionsHigh fires above (held 10 minutes). Many 'idle' is a pool holding connections open: normal until it nears the limit. 'idle in transaction' that stays above 0 is an app that opened a transaction and forgot it (it also blocks vacuum). Series at zero are hidden.

panels.title: Longest open transaction, by state
panels.description: Age of the oldest open transaction in each state, from the exporter's pg_stat_activity query. 'active' is a running query: seconds is normal for a report, minutes means a stuck or runaway query. 'idle in transaction' should stay near 0: a long one holds locks, blocks vacuum and bloats tables. No alert rule; the cure is the app's code (runbook PostgresConnectionsHigh has the pg_stat_activity query).

targets.expr: max by (state) (pg_stat_activity_max_tx_duration{job="service", instance="postgres", state=~"active|idle in transaction.*"})

panels.title: Locks held, by mode
panels.description: Locks currently held, by mode, over all databases. A few access-share and row-exclusive locks are the normal background of live queries. A climbing access-exclusive or share lock count means DDL or a migration is running. The exporter counts locks held, not waiters, so a blocked query does not show here: look at the longest open transaction. No alert rule.

panels.title: Is it healthy? Transactions, cache, errors
Transactions per second, by database
panels.description: Committed and rolled-back transactions per second: the rate of the database's work (RED rate and errors). Rollbacks should be a small fraction of commits; a line that rises with a failing app is its errors. Flat zero for a database that should be busy means the app cannot reach it. No alert rule.

panels.title: Cache hit ratio, by database
panels.description: Share of block reads served from shared_buffers instead of the OS or disk. An OLTP workload sits at 95-99 % or more; a falling line means the working set outgrew shared_buffers and queries read from disk. A gap is a window with no reads at all. No alert rule.

targets.expr: sum by (datname) (rate(pg_stat_database_blks_hit{job="service", instance="postgres", datname!~"template.*"}[$__rate_interval])) / (sum by (datname) (rate(pg_stat_database_blks_hit{job="service", instance="postgres", datname!~"template.*"}[$__rate_interval])) + sum by (datname) (rate(pg_stat_database_blks_read{job="service", instance="postgres", datname!~"template.*"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: Deadlocks in the last hour, by database
panels.description: Deadlocks Postgres resolved by killing one transaction, over a trailing hour. Should be 0: each one is an app error and a sign of two code paths locking rows in opposite order. No alert rule.

panels.title: Write load, temp files and WAL
Rows written per second
panels.description: Rows inserted, updated and deleted per second, all databases. The write load behind the growth and WAL panels: a runaway insert loop shows here first. No alert rule.

panels.title: Temp files written
panels.description: Bytes per second queries spilled to temporary files because a sort or hash outgrew work_mem. Occasional bursts are fine; a steady stream means a query needs an index or more work_mem, and it adds disk writes. No alert rule.

panels.title: WAL archived, and segments waiting
panels.description: WAL segments (16 MiB each) Postgres archived to the bucket in the last hour, archive_command failures, and segments queued in pg_wal. archive_timeout forces a switch every 15 minutes, so about 4 an hour is the idle floor, not the WAL rate (the exporter has no WAL-byte or checkpoint counters). Failures above 0 or a queue that does not return to 0 means B2 is unreachable: rule PostgresOffsiteArchiveStale fires after an hour. Past 4 GiB queued, pgBackRest drops segments.

panels.title: How big is it, and how fast does it grow?
Database size, by database
panels.description: Size of each database. The dashed line is 5e9 bytes, rule PostgresDatabaseLarge (1 hour): a planning signal for the application databases. The postgres database is shown (about 8 MB) but the rule leaves it and the templates out.

panels.title: Growth over the trailing 24 h and 7 d, by database
panels.description: How much each application database grew over the 24 hours and the 7 days before each point (size then minus size back then). The dashed line is 1e9 bytes in 24 hours, rule PostgresDatabaseGrowingFast (30 minutes). Use the 7 d line for the trend: steady slope is fine, a sudden step is a bulk load or a runaway. Negative after a vacuum full or a big delete.

targets.expr: max by (datname) (pg_database_size_bytes{job="service", instance="postgres", datname!~"postgres|template.*"}) - max by (datname) (pg_database_size_bytes{job="service", instance="postgres", datname!~"postgres|template.*"} offset 1d)

max by (datname) (pg_database_size_bytes{job="service", instance="postgres", datname!~"postgres|template.*"}) - max by (datname) (pg_database_size_bytes{job="service", instance="postgres", datname!~"postgres|template.*"} offset 7d)

panels.title: Root disk used, over time
panels.description: CT 130's root disk used, from the Proxmox API (data, WAL, the last 3 dumps). The dashed line is 80 %, rule PostgresDiskFilling (30 minutes). Fix: grow disk_gb in proxmox/opentofu/postgres.tf (online). The CT's CPU and memory are on the Host and guest board (pick 'postgres').

panels.title: Disk runway, days until full
panels.description: Days until the root disk is full if the last 7 days of change continue (linear, capped at 365; a disk that is not growing reads 365). The dashed lines mark 7 days (orange) and 30 days (green): under 30 is worth a plan. Warns weeks before rule PostgresDiskFilling, which fires only at 80 % full.

panels.title: Off-site copy to Backblaze B2: is it current?
Daily job, last success
panels.description: Time since pg-offsite-daily last completed (a full backup when due, the repo size, the guard). Red from 30 hours is rule PostgresOffsiteDailyFailing (30 minutes). When it stops, the repo size and full-backup series on this board go stale. Runbook: PostgresOffsiteDailyFailing.

panels.title: Guard expired, last 24 h
panels.description: 1 when the repo passed 9 GB and the daily job expired it down to one full backup within the last 24 hours (rule PostgresOffsiteGuardExpired, fires for a day). The restore window is then 0-3 days instead of 3-6 until the repo shrinks. 0 is the normal state.

targets.expr: count(pg_offsite_guard_last_expire_timestamp_seconds{job="service", instance="postgres"} > 0 and time() - pg_offsite_guard_last_expire_timestamp_seconds{job="service", instance="postgres"} < 86400) or vector(0)

panels.title: Full backups in the repo
panels.description: Full backups pgBackRest keeps in the bucket. Two or more is the steady state (restore window 3-6 days); one means a newly created repo or a guard expiry (window 0-3 days). Orange until the second full is taken. No alert rule beyond PostgresOffsiteGuardExpired.

panels.title: Newest archived WAL segment, age
panels.description: Time since the last WAL segment reached the bucket, as a saw-tooth: it climbs to at most 15 minutes (archive_timeout) and drops on each upload. The dashed line is 1 hour, rule PostgresOffsiteArchiveStale (5 minutes). A line that keeps climbing past it is B2 unreachable, a revoked key or a full bucket.

panels.title: Off-site copy: full backups and repo size
Newest full backup and daily job, age
panels.description: Age of the newest full backup (a full is taken every third day at 04:00 WIB) and of the daily job's last completed run (every day at 04:00 WIB). The dashed line is 4 days, rule PostgresOffsiteFullBackupOld (30 minutes); the daily job's own limit is 30 hours, rule PostgresOffsiteDailyFailing (tile above). The daily line should saw-tooth under a day, the full under 3 days.

panels.title: Off-site repo size against the 10 GB free tier
panels.description: Size of the pgBackRest repo in B2. The dashed lines are 8e9 bytes (orange), rule PostgresOffsiteRepoLarge (15 minutes), and 9e9 (red), where the daily job expires down to one full backup. B2's free tier is 10 GB, and its $0 cap refuses writes at the limit. Steady state is about 4-5 GB; it was 110 MB right after archiving went live (2026-11-09), so expect a climb. B2's own bucket size, including hidden versions, is only in its web UI.

panels.title: PostgreSQL: errors, fatals and panics
panels.description: Error-level lines from CT 130's journal (syslog identifier postgres): ERROR statements, FATAL connection failures and PANICs, plus anything the journal marks error or critical. A few ERROR lines from application SQL (duplicate keys) are normal; FATAL or PANIC, or a burst, is the story behind an alert. Not checked by --verify-live.

targets.expr: _stream:{_HOSTNAME="postgres"} (level:(error or critical) or ERROR or FATAL or PANIC)
